summary: This is an April 1st joke RFC proposing a new ICMP message that a router or host could use to tell a host to slow down when it ignores other signals like packet loss and ECN. It is humorous and not for real use.

eli5.summary: This is a joke: a router would send a message telling a computer to calm down and send slower when it ignores hints.

questions: what is really explicit congestion notification
subtitle: An April Fools' approach to telling hosts to slow down, very explicitly.

tldr.problem: Some hosts ignore Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) and packet loss signals to slow down, continuing to send too fast.
tldr.mechanism: This April Fools' RFC proposes a new ICMP message (Really Explicit Congestion Notification) that routers can send with a 4-byte text field, explicitly telling a host to reduce its transmission rate in words rather than silent packet drops.
tldr.outcome: This is a humorous April 1st document, not a real protocol. It parodies the limitations of ECN by proposing literal messages.

today: RFC 7514 is an Experimental RFC published on April 1, 2015, as an April Fools' Day joke. It is not a real protocol and was never intended for actual deployment.

sections.title: The Problem with Silent Signals
sections.content: RFC 7514 proposes Really Explicit Congestion Notification (RECN), a tongue-in-cheek solution to hosts that stubbornly ignore both packet loss and Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) [RFC3168]. Some senders continue to transmit at unfair rates regardless of congestion signals. RECN delivers congestion information in a form a host cannot miss: a 4-byte ASCII message in an ICMP packet.
sections.eli5: If a host ignores both dropped packets and polite hints, the router sends an actual message, 4 letters long, telling it to slow down.

sections.title: RECN Message Structure
sections.content: An RECN message is an ICMP packet with a 32-bit Explicit Notification field containing a 4-byte ASCII value. The type is IPv4 type 4 (reusing the deprecated ICMP Source Quench type) and IPv6 type 201. A router SHOULD NOT send an RECN message for every dropped packet, but rather for each packet in a burst from a congestion-causing sender. The specification humorously suggests that routers can form short sentences composed of different 4-byte RECN messages and escalate the content if the host does not respond, with no upper bound on intensity.
sections.eli5: The message is 4 letters, sent in an ICMP packet. A router can send one for each packet in a burst, and can even send sentences of multiple 4-letter words to naughty hosts.

sections.title: Implementer Advice and Deployment
sections.content: The RFC notes that implementers are free to choose their own 4-letter words during the experimental period. The specification advises that if the system has text-to-speech, the message should be converted to sound and audibly rendered; if muted, a pop-up will do. Hosts must verify the quoted message corresponds to an active flow to prevent spoofing attacks. The document wryly references RFC 3514 ("The Security Flag in the IPv4 Header"), implying attackers must set the security flag when sending RECN messages.
sections.eli5: If your computer can speak, the message is spoken out loud. If it is muted, a pop-up appears. Attackers must follow the rules too.

sections.title: Inspiration and Status
sections.content: RECN was inspired by the deprecated ICMP Source Quench message [RFC6633], which was removed from the specification because it was ineffective and could be abused. This RFC acknowledges that relationship by reusing the same ICMP type. The document is Experimental, with the experiment concluding two years after publication. No real-world implementations were anticipated.
sections.eli5: This idea builds on an old system called Source Quench that nobody uses anymore. It is a joke about what a more literal approach would look like.

references.text: Ramakrishnan, K., Floyd, S., and D. Black, "The Addition of Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) to IP", RFC 3168, September 2001.
